figures.caption: Fig. 1 Representation of an oscillator exhibiting a stable period orbit in the uncoupled state. Left Voltage trace showing the phase zero as the peak of the potential. Right The stable orbit can be represented as a limit cycle in phase space with θ = 0 and θ = π corresponding, respectively, to the spike times of the voltage trace and to times half a period, T/2, from the spike times.
Fig. 2 Voltage traces corresponding to an N-oscillator system exhibiting a symmetric N−cluster phase-locked or splay state solution where the adjacent phase differences are constant and identical.

Fig. 3 Bifurcation curves in (Iapp, gM ) parameter space. Red curves correspond to fold bifurcation of equilibria, blue to Hopf bifurcation. (A). Full two-parameter bifurcation diagram (B). Zoomed-in view near the red curves, highlighting the region relevant to our analysis. As gM increases, the two fold curves merge at a cusp point (labelled CP). Additionally, we see a curve of Hopf points emerging from the BT point.

Fig. 4 One parameter bifurcation diagrams as a function of current (Iapp) for the RTM model. The red (black) curves indicate stable (unstable) equilibrium points. The green (blue) curves show the maximum and minimum voltages along the stable (unstable) periodic orbits. (A) Below the BT bifurcation point in Figure 3 (gM = 0). The oscillations are born via a saddle-node on an invariant circle as Iapp is increased. Thus the model exhibits class I excitability. (B) Above the BT bifurcation point (gM = 5). The oscillations are born via a subcritical Hopf bifurcation (labelled HB). Although the limit points still exist, the branch of periodic solutions are emerging from the Hopf point rather than the limit point. Thus the model exhibits class II excitability. Numerical limitations prevented us from demonstrating the connection between the blue curves.

Fig. 6 Multiple stable cluster solutions obtained for a network of reduced Traub-Miles model neurons of sizes N = 10, 12, 15 and 24, with global homogeneous coupling and gM = 0 (high ACh). The voltage traces are presented for a (A) 4−cluster, (D) 6−cluster and (G) 5−cluster solutions. A stable 4−cluster solution is illustrated for a network of (B) 24 cells and (C) 12 cells, both associated with ψ = π 2 . A stable 6−cluster is illustrated in a network of (E) 24 cells and (F) 12 cells, both associated with ψ = π 3 . (H) A stable 5−cluster solution is illustrated for a network of 15 cells associated with ψ = 2π 5 . (I)A different stable 5−cluster is illustrated for a network of 10 cells with ψ = 8π 5 . The order of cluster firing is discussed in the main text.

Fig. 7 Synchronization of a network of RTM model neurons with global homogeneous coupling, when gM = 5 (low ACh). (A) The voltage traces associated for the synchronized (1−cluster) solution. The synchronized solution is illustrated for a network of (B) 24 cells, (C) 15 cells, (D) 12 cells and (E) 10 cells through raster plots.

Fig. 8 Demonstration of splay state solutions for RTM networks equipped with distance-dependent coupling (p = 0.5, k = ⌊N/2⌋) with gM = 5 (low ACh). (A) A splay solution for a network of 12 cells, spiking with a phase difference ψ = π 6 . (B) A splay solution for 16 cells with a phase difference ψ = π 8 . (C) A splay solution obtained for a network of 24 neurons with ψ = π 12 . In each case, the cells fire in the order of 1 − 2 − 3 − · · · −N as illustrated through the raster plots.

Fig. 9 Splay state solutions for a network of RTM model neurons, equipped with nearest neighbour coupling, with gM = 5 (low ACh). (A) A network of 7 cells exhibiting a 7−cluster solution with ψ = 12π 7 . (B) A network of 5 cells exhibiting a 5−cluster solution with ψ = 2π 5 .

Fig. 10 Multiple stable n−cluster solutions are obtained for a network RTM model neurons with nearest neighbour coupling and gM = 5 (low ACh). (A),(D)& (G) display the representative voltage traces for each solution. Panels (B) and (C) illustrate the 6−cluster solution in a network of 12 and 24 cells resp, with ψ = π 3 . Panels (E) and (F) demonstrate the 8−cluster solution in a network of 8 and 24 cells resp with ψ = π 4 . Panels (H) and (I) illustrate the 12−cluster in a network of 12 and 24 cells resp, with ψ = π 6

Fig. 11 Multistability in a network of 24 RTM model neurons with globally homogeneous coupling and gM = 0 (high ACh). (A) The network is initialized in a stable 4−cluster with a firing order: C1 − C2 − C3−C4, where Ci = {i, i+4, . . . , 19+ i}. (B) A transient perturbation, in the form a current pulse applied to a subset of cells, can switch the network to a stable 4−cluster solution where the cells belonging to C2 and C4 change to {2, 10, 12, 14, 22, 24} and {4, 6, 8, 16, 18, 20}, respectively. (C) Applying the pulse to a different subset of the cells alters the firing order to C1 − C4 − C2 − C3. (D) The network is initialized in a stable 6−cluster with a firing order: C1 −C2 −C3 −C4 −C5 −C6, where Ci = {i, i+6, . . . , 17+ i}. (E) A transient perturbation, in the form a current pulse applied to subset of the cells, alters the firing order to C1 − C2 − C6 − C3 − C4 − C5. (F) The perturbation can also switch the network to a stable 6−cluster solution where the cells belonging to cluster C6, C2 and C4 change to {8, 10, 20, 22},{2, 12, 14, 24} and {4, 6, 16, 18} and the firing order changes to C1−C2−C3−C6−C5−C4. (G) Applying a perturbation to a different subset of cells can also switch the network to a stable 6−cluster solution where the cells belonging to cluster C6, C2 and C4 change to {6, 11, 16, 18},{2, 13, 20, 24} and {4, 8, 10, 22}.

Fig. 12 Multistability in a network of RTM model neurons, equipped with global distance dependent coupling (p = 0.5), when gM = 0 (high ACh). In each case, the network is initialized in a stable cluster solution and a transient perturbation is applied to a subset of the cells during time t ∈ [8000, 8050]. (A) Network of 8 cells is initialized in a stable 4−cluster solution ( ψ = π 2 ) . (B) The perturbation reverses the firing order of the spiking cells from (A), switching the network to a different stable 4−cluster solution( ψ = 3π 2 ) . (C) A perturbation applied to a different subset of cells, can switch the initial state in (A) to a stable 8−cluster ( ψ = 7π 4 ) . (D) Network of 24 cells is initialized in a stable 4−cluster solution ( ψ = π 2 ) . (E) The perturbation switches the network in (D) to a different stable 4−cluster solution (ψ = 3π 2 ) (F) The network in (D) can also switch to a stable 8−cluster ( ψ = 7π 4 ) .

Fig. 13 Multistability in a network of RTM model neurons with distance dependent coupling and gM = 5 (low ACh). A transient perturbation is applied during time t ∈ [8000, 8050] to a network initialized in a stable splay solution. (A) Network of 12 cells, initialized in a stable splay solution( ψ = π 6 ) , synchronizes when 6 of the cells are perturbed transiently. (B)Network of 16 cells, initialized in a stable splay solution ( ψ = π 8 ) , synchronizes when 8 of the cells are perturbed transiently. (C) Network of 24 cells, initialized in a stable splay solution ( ψ = π 12 ) , synchronizes when 12 of the cells are perturbed transiently.

Fig. 14 Demonstration of possible transitions between stable cluster solutions when gM = 5 (low ACh), for a network of 24 RTM model neurons, equipped with nearest neighbour coupling. (A) The network is initialized in a stable 6− cluster solution (ψ = π 3 ) (B) A transient perturbation applied to 3 cells in the network, can switch the solution in (A) to a stable 8−cluster solution associated with ψ = π 4 (C) A transient perturbation applied to 4 cells in the network, can switch the solution in (B) to a stable 12−cluster solution associated with ψ = π 6 (D) A transient perturbation applied to 12 cells in the network, can synchronize the network. Transient perturbations applied to different subset of the cells in the network initialized in (A), (B) or (C), can also synchronize them.
